description: Somos AZGARD, un equipo multidisciplinario de Hidalgo del Parral, Chihuahua, enfocado en ingeniería, programación, simulación y desarrollo de videojuegos. Participamos en Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer con el objetivo de desarrollar un simulador educativo de operaciones espaciales, basado en principios científicos, donde los usuarios puedan administrar una colonia lunar, resolver emergencias y tomar decisiones de ingeniería.
summary: Developed by team AZGARD, TÝR is an educational space mission game that helps children explore the decisions behind human exploration of Mars. Players progress from introductory training toward managing a human outpost, considering competing needs such as life support, energy, radiation protection, communications, and food production. Our prototype combines interactive mission interfaces with a decision engine and a solar weather scenario informed by NASA resources. NASA DONKI integration supports recent solar flare information, while a clearly identified historical scenario provides an alternative when recent data is unavailable. Through choices and feedback, players explore how protecting the crew can affect other mission priorities. The project addresses the challenge by turning scientific information and engineering tradeoffs into an accessible learning experience. Its purpose is to encourage scientific curiosity, systems thinking, and evidence-based decisions while making the complexity of sustaining human life on Mars easier to understand
details: TÝR, developed by team AZGARD, is a browser-based educational mission trainer about human exploration of Mars. It introduces children to scientific concepts through decisions, visual mission contexts, and feedback. Its journey connects curiosity about space with training, travel, arrival, and the challenges of sustaining a human outpost. The campaign interface includes mission briefings, decision situations, resource displays, and debriefing screens. Missions M01 through M11 contain 110 decision situations, organized as ten per mission. A separate M12 scenario includes a decision engine and NASA solar weather integration. Together, these components form the educational prototype. The central learning challenge is interdependence. Life support, radiation protection, energy, communications, and food production compete for attention and resources. Players consider how protecting the crew can affect other mission objectives, developing systems thinking and evidence-based decision skills. NASA DONKI supplies solar flare information for the space weather component. Recent observations are distinguished from a historical X8.7 flare scenario dated May 14, 2024, and from an offline fallback. A separate NASA report about the May 20, 2024 radiation event at Mars provides scientific context. Flare classification is not a direct measurement of astronaut radiation dose. The development stack includes TypeScript, React, Phaser, Vite, HTML, and CSS, with Node.js and npm supporting development and builds. React supports the interface and mission flow, while Phaser is the project’s game presentation engine. The creative approach combines a narrative journey with decisions informed by real space science. The intended impact is greater curiosity about STEM and a clearer understanding of the systems involved in human space exploration.
